title: Multi-omics analysis reveals differential benefits of immunotherapy±chemotherapy based on detailed smoking history in advanced non-small cell lung cancer
author: Xinan Wang; Biagio Ricciuti; Arielle Elkrief; Joao V Alessi; Alessandro Di Federico; Federica Pecci; Mizuki Nishino; Doga Gulhan; Guruprasad Ananda; Scott J Rodig; Lynette Sholl; Bruce Johnson; Xihong Lin; Adam Schoenfeld; Mark M Awad; David Christiani
text:
Abstract
Background
Despite immunotherapy±chemotherapy has transformed the therapeutic landscape for patients with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), critical questions remain regarding how detailed smoking history affects the evolving treatment options and the underlying molecular mechanisms driving these effects.
Methods
We analyzed 4157 patients with advanced NSCLC who were treated with immunotherapy monotherapy (IO alone) (n=2768) or chemoimmunotherapy (chemo-IO) (n=1389) at the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute and Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (2010–2023). Associations between detailed smoking history (status and cumulative pack-years) and clinical outcomes were assessed using multivariable analyses. First-line chemo-IO versus IO alone was compared in programmed death receptor ligand 1 (PD-L1) Tumor Proportion Score (TPS) of ≥50% EGFR/ALK wild-type patients. Tobacco smoking-related mutational signature (TSMS) was inferred from the targeted next generation sequencing (NGS) panel. We investigated relationships between detailed smoking history and tumor genomics/transcriptomics, PD-L1 expression, tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes, and circulating plasma proteomics.
Results
In patients receiving IO alone, both smoking status and intensity showed dose-dependent associations with improved response and survival outcomes. In contrast, among patients receiving chemo-IO, smoking history did not affect initial response but patients with active (HR=0.73, 95% CI 0.57 to 0.94, p=0.01) and heavy tobacco use (HR=0.76, 95% CI 0.62 to 0.93, p=0.001) showed improved progression-free survival (PFS), and a trend toward improved overall survival (OS). Importantly, these associations remained independent of STK11, KEAP1, and KRAS co-mutation status. In patients with PD-L1 TPS of ≥50% lacking EGFR/ALK alterations, patients who do not smoke derived significant benefit from first-line chemo-IO versus IO alone with higher response rates (70.0% vs 23.9%, p=0.001), prolonged PFS (median PFS 9.5 vs 3.7 months, HR=0.51, 95% CI 0.27 to 0.95, p=0.04), and a trend toward prolonged OS, while patients who smoke showed comparable outcomes with either strategy. TSMS independently predicted improved outcomes of IO alone, even after tumor mutational burden (TMB) adjustment. Molecular analyses revealed associations between tobacco use and higher TMB, increased tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (CD8+, PD-1+, CD8+PD-1+, FOXP3+) and distinct plasma protein profiles involved in immune signaling pathways (CCL7, CXCL17, CDCP1, TNFRSF6B).
Conclusions
Detailed smoking history provides crucial insights for optimizing IO selection in advanced NSCLC through mechanistic alterations in both the tumor microenvironment and systemic plasma protein profiles.
Keywords: Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer, Biomarker, Immunotherapy, Tumor infiltrating lymphocyte - TIL, Tumor mutation burden - TMB
WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ON THIS TOPIC
Smoking history shows a dose-response association with improved response and clinical outcomes to immune checkpoint inhibition alone in patients with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC).
WHAT THIS STUDY ADDS
Smoking history does not affect initial response, but patients with active or heavy tobacco use show prolonged progression-free survival with a trend toward improved overall survival on chemoimmunotherapy (chemo-IO), independent of STK11, KEAP1, and KRAS co-mutations.
In first-line treatment of programmed death receptor ligand 1 (PD-L1) Tumor Proportion Score (TPS) of ≥50% patients without EGFR/ALK alterations, patients who do not smoked tend to benefit more from chemo-IO, while patients with a smoking history show comparable outcomes with chemo-IO or IO alone.
Tobacco smoking mutational signature from clinical next-generation sequencing panels (NGS) independently predicts IO response, providing valuable molecular information when self-reported smoking history is unavailable.
Tobacco smoking is associated with higher tumor mutational burden, higher PD-L1 TPS, increased tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes, elevated circulating plasma proteins in immune-related pathways, and altered transcriptional signatures in cancer metabolism and signaling transport.
HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH, PRACTICE OR POLICY
Our study provides a comprehensive analysis of how cigarette smoking history influences IO outcomes in NSCLC via complex molecular mechanisms. These findings have clinical implications for personalized treatment selection and suggest new directions for biomarker development.
Introduction
Immune checkpoint inhibition (ICI) targeting programmed death protein 1 (PD -1)/programmed death receptor ligand 1 (PD-L1) axis, either as immunotherapy monotherapy (IO alone) or in combination with chemotherapy (chemo-IO), has transformed the therapeutic landscape for patients with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Despite these advances, critical questions remain regarding how detailed cigarette smoking history, including both smoking status and cumulative smoking pack-years (PYs), impacts the evolving treatment options and the underlying molecular mechanisms driving these effects.
While studies have demonstrated that patients with a smoking history show enhanced response and survival with ICI monotherapy, likely due to tobacco-induced elevation in tumor mutational burden (TMB) and generation of neoantigens,1,7 the treatment landscape has evolved with chemo-IO emerging as the standard first-line therapy for a large fraction of patients with advanced NSCLC.8,11 Therefore, defining the relationship between smoking history and different treatment modalities has become increasingly important for clinical decision-making. Such insights may help identify patient subgroups that will benefit from upfront treatment intensification versus those that could potentially avoid unnecessary toxicity associated with chemotherapy.
Beyond establishing the impact of smoking history on treatment outcomes, identifying the underlying biological mechanisms is crucial. While clinical trials have primarily relied on established biomarkers such as PD-L1 Tumor Proportion Score (TPS) and TMB,1 3 5 emerging molecular features, including derived neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (dNLR), plasma proteomic profiles, tumor aneuploidy, mutational signatures, and tumor-infiltrating immune cell abundance, have shown promise in predicting immunotherapy response.910 12,16 However, little is known about how these molecular features are influenced by different habits of tobacco use and how they impact the efficacy of ICI alongside PD-L1 TPS and TMB.
To address these knowledge gaps, we investigated the associations between detailed smoking history and ICI efficacy in 4157 patients with advanced NSCLC treated with IO alone or chemo-IO. By integrating clinical outcomes with tumor genomics, transcriptomics, immune cell infiltration, and plasma proteomics, we propose to elucidate how smoking patterns influence treatment responses and to identify potential biomarkers for treatment stratification (figure 1).
Methods
Study population
Consecutive patients with NSCLC who were treated with IO alone or chemo-IO at the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute (DFCI) and Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSKCC) between 2010 and 2023 were included. Patients who have received PD-L1 blockade (with or without group). Baseline covariates, including age, sex, cigarette smoking status (never, former, and current smoking status), cumulative cigarette smoking PYs, lung cancer histology, Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group Performance Status (ECOG PS), and lines of treatment, were well annotated. Smoking history throughout this study refers to cigarette smoking. Based on cumulative PYs, patients were categorized as having never smoked or having a light (>0–20 PYs), moderate (≥20–40 PYs), or heavy (≥40 PYs) cigarette smoking history.17 18 Objective response was evaluated using the RECIST V.1.1 criteria by board-certified thoracic radiologists. Progression-free survival (PFS) was measured from treatment initiation until progression or death from any cause. Patients alive and progression-free at the date of data cut-off were censored at the date of last radiographic assessment. Overall survival (OS) was calculated from treatment initiation until death from any cause or the date of the last contact. Patientsalive at the date of data cut-off were censored at the date of last contact. Patients from the SU2C (Stand Up To Cancer) lung cancer cohort were included to investigate the relationship between smoking history and tumor transcriptomics, leveraging this collaborative research initiative that collects comprehensive genomic, transcriptomic, clinical, and treatment data from patients with NSCLC.16
Statistical analyses
Linear correlations were evaluated using Pearson’s correlation test, and categorical variables were evaluated using the Wilcoxon and Kruskal-Wallis tests. Time-to-event distributions were estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method, and log-rank tests were used to test for differences in event time distributions. Median follow-up was calculated with the reverse Kaplan-Meier method. Multivariable logistic and Cox proportional hazards models were used to evaluate the association between smoking history and clinical outcomes, with patients who do not smoke as the reference group, adjusting for potential confounders of age, sex, histology, lines of treatment, ECOG PS, PD-L1 TPS, and institution (online supplemental figure 1A). Inverse probability treatment weighting (IPTW) was applied to account for PD-L1 TPS missingness, as previously described in a study by Cole and Hernan.19 In patients with PD-L1 TPS of ≥50% lacking EGFR/ALK alterations, subgroup analyses based on smoking history were conducted to compare the efficacy of IO alone versus chemo-IO in the first-line setting. To minimize potential treatment selection bias, we applied IPTW based on factors that could influence treatment choice, including age, histology, ECOG PS, smoking status, and institution. All analyses used two-sided tests, with a significance set at p<0.05.
Molecular analyses were conducted in different subsets of patients, based on data availability (online supplemental figure 1B). Tumor genomic profiling was performed using OncoPanel (DFCI) and MSK-IMPACT (MSKCC).20,22 TMB was harmonized across platforms for comparison, as previously published in a study by Ricciuti et al.13 PD-L1 TPS was assessed by immunohistochemistry (IHC) using validated antibodies (E1L3N, 22C3, 28–8, and SP263) in 2963 (71.3%) patients from the DFCI and MSKCC. Immune cell infiltration in 691 patients from the DFCI was assessed using multiplex immunofluorescence with antibodies against PD-L1 (clone E1L3N), PD-1 (clone EPR4877(2)), CD8 (clone 4B11), FOXP3 (clone D608R), Cytokeratin (clone AE1/AE3), and DAPI (nuclear counterstain) regardless of therapy received. Representative images can be found from our previous work.13 Measurements included intratumoral and tumor-stroma interface regions and their combined total area. Circulating biomarkers include dNLR and plasma proteomics. Pretreatment dNLR was extracted from the medical records of 3884 patients from the DFCI and MSKCC. Plasma proteomics were measured using the Olink Explore 3072 panel for 152 patients from the DFCI. The panel includes 2941 proteins across eight panels in cardiometabolism, inflammation, neurology, and oncology. Transcriptomic analysis was restricted to 111 patients with lung adenocarcinoma from the SU2C lung cancer cohort to ensure an adequate sample size and tumor homogeneity.16
Tobacco smoking-related mutational signature analysis
Mutational signature analysis was performed using Signature Multivariate Analysis (SigMA),23 a method optimized for panel-based sequencing data, on samples from the DFCI cohort where individual-level genomic data were available. SigMA analyzes 96 mutation types based on six substitutions and their nucleotide contexts, taking histology into account, and was specifically trained for OncoPanel data. SigMA requires >5 SNVsonline supplemental figure 1B) but very few cases with other histologies. Therefore, adjusted clinical analysis was restricted to lung adenocarcinoma to ensure adequate sample size and reliable associations. Tobacco smoking signature (SBS4) enrichment was determined using a likelihood threshold of 0.5 against COSMIC V.3 signatures.24,26
Differentially expressed protein analysis
The association between smoking status (ever vs never) and each Olink-normalized protein expression was analyzed using linear regression with adjustment for age, sex, and histology. Multiple testing was adjusted using the effective number of tests method,27 28 with the significance threshold set at p<0.05/ENT (number of principal components explaining 95% of the protein variance). Incremental changes in the differentially expressed proteins (DEPs) according to smoking status (never, former, and current) were further evaluated using an adjusted analysis of variance test. Gene-set enrichment analysis was performed based on the results of the DEP analysis using the OlinkAnalyze R package. We further explored the predictive effect of DEPs on the initial response to IO alone by using logistic regression, adjusting for baseline covariates and PD-L1 TPS.
Tumor microenvironment analysis
Tumor microenvironment (TME) was analyzed based on RNA sequencing data from the SU2C cohort, using the IOBR package.16 29 Cell fractions were quantified from bulk tissue gene expression profiles using CIBERSORT,30 and gene signature scores from curated databases covering TME-associated, tumor-metabolism, and tumor-intrinsic signatures were estimated using the principal component analysis method.31
Results
Patient characteristics
A total of 4157 patients with advanced NSCLC were identified, of whom 2768 (66.6%) received IO alone and 1389 (33.4%) received chemo-IO. Median follow-up time for the entire cohort was 44.0 months (95% CI 42.5 to 45.4), with 32.3 months (95% CI 30.7 to 34.1) for the chemo-IO group and 51.8 months (95% CI 49.8 to 54.8) for the IO alone group. The cohort included 51.7% female patients, with lung adenocarcinoma as the predominant histology (78.6%) (table 1). Compared with IO alone, patients treated with chemo-IO were more likely to have lung adenocarcinoma (81.6% vs 77.1%), ECOG PS 0 (27.1% vs 16.3%), and PD-L1 TPS of<1% (45.6% vs 18.1%), and in the first-line setting (90.8% vs 36.1%) (online supplemental table 3). In the combined cohort, 3212 patients (77.5%) reported a history of smoking, 634 (15.3%) had never smoked, and smoking history was unavailable in 303 patients (7.3%) (table 1). Among those with a smoking history, 744 (23.1%) were actively smoking at diagnosis with a median exposure of 40 PYs, whereas 2471 (76.9%) were formerly smoking with a median exposure of 30 PYs. Patients with a smoking history were more frequently treated with IO alone than with chemo-IO (80.0% vs 72.6%, (online supplemental table 3). First-line treatment was administrated to 54.9% of the patients with a history of smoking compared with 40% of the patients who do not smoke.

Dose-response association between smoking history and IO monotherapy outcomes
Consistent with our prior work, patients with a smoking history showed higher response to IO alone (never: 8.7%, former: 21.6%, current: 27.5%, p<0.001; figure 2A). Both formerly (median PFS (mPFS)=2.9 months, median OS (mOS)=11.3 months) and actively smoking (mPFS=3.6 months, mOS=13 months) patients demonstrated longer PFS and OS compared with those who have never smoked (mPFS=2.1 months, mOS=10.5 months, figure 2B,C). A dose-response relationship was observed between cumulative smoking PYs and clinical outcomes of IO alone, with patients who had heavy tobacco use (≥40 PYs) showing the highest objective response rate (ORR) (24.4%), longest mPFS (3.5 months), and mOS (12.7 months) (figure 2D–F).
In multivariable analyses adjusted for PD-L1 TPS and other clinicopathological factors, current smoking status maintained a higher ORR compared with patients who had never smoked (OR=2.89, 95% CI 1.83 to 4.66, p<0.001, (online supplemental table 4). Patients who do not smoke showed significantly shorter PFS compared with patients who were formerly (HR=0.67, 95% CI 0.58 to 0.78, p<0.001) and actively smoking (HR=0.64, 95% CI 0.54 to 0.77, p<0.001, (online supplemental table 5), with a similar trend in OS (online supplemental table 6). Cumulative smoking PYs showed a dose-response relationship with improved ORR, PFS, and OS in patients with heavy tobacco use compared with those who had never smoked (online supplemental tables 7–9). These associations remained consistent in sensitivity analyses after adjusting for PD-L1 TPS missingness (online supplemental tables 10–15).
Chemo-immunotherapy response independent of smoking history but improved survival in patients with heavy tobacco use
In contrast, smoking status (never: 39.3%, former: 37.7%, current: 43.0%, p=0.19, figure 3A) and intensity (never: 39.3%, light: 34.8%, moderate: 36.6%, heavy: 43.8%, p=0.11, figure 3D) were not associated with initial response to chemo-IO, and they were confirmed in the multivariable association analyses (online supplemental tables 16 and 19). Long-term PFS survival benefit was only observed in patients who were actively smoking (mPFS=7.1 months, HR=0.68, 95% CI 0.55 to 0.85, p<0.01, figure 3B) and in those with heavy tobacco use (mPFS=7.1 months, HR=0.79, 95% CI 0.66 to 0.94, p<0.01, figure 3E) as compared with patients who do not smoke, confirmed by multivariable analyses (online supplemental tables 17,20). This group also showed a trend toward improved OS in the multivariable analyses (HR=0.80, 95% CI 0.64 to 1.00, p=0.06, figure 3F, online supplemental tables 18 and 21). Sensitivity analyses adjusted for PD-L1 TPS missingness confirmed these associations (online supplemental tables 22–27).
Smoking history maintains independent predictive value beyond STK11, KEAP1 and KRAS co-mutations
Given the strong associations between tobacco exposure and STK11, KEAP1, and KRAS co-mutations that serve as predictive biomarkers for IO,32 we investigated whether smoking history retains independent predictive value for clinical outcomes. As expected, mutation prevalence increases with tobacco use. Patients who currently smoke had the highest rates of KRAS, STK11, and KEAP1 mutations (40.2%, 24.2%, and 22.7%, respectively) compared with patients who do not smoke (14.2%, 5.7%, and 4.2%, respectively, online supplemental table 28). Similarly, co-mutations KRASmut/STK11mut and KRASmut/KEAP1mut were more frequent in actively smoking (10.4% and 7.3%, respectively) than in patients who do not smoke (1.4% and 0.7%, respectively, online supplemental table 28). This pattern was consistent with smoking PYs, where mutation frequencies generally increased with tobacco exposure intensity (online supplemental table 29).
In multivariable analyses adjusting for both smoking and mutations, smoking independently predicted worse outcomes for IO alone with dose-response associations, while long-term survival benefit from chemo-IO was only observed in heavy and active tobacco users across both smoking status and PYs (online supplemental tables 30–35), confirming the main results.
Despite their similar associations with smoking history, mutations showed distinct predictive patterns. For IO alone, STK11mut independently predicted shorter PFS (HR=1.20, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.41, p=0.04, online supplemental table 31) and OS (HR=1.31, 95% CI 1.10 to 1.57, p=0.003, online supplemental table 32) but not ORR (online supplemental table 30), while KEAP1mut only predicted worse OS compared with wild type (online supplemental tables 30–32). In contrast, for chemo-IO, STK11, KEAP1, and KRAS co-mutations independently predicted worse clinical outcomes across all endpoints (online supplemental tables 33–35). Patients with KRASmut/STK11mut (ORR: OR=0.43, 95% CI 0.26 to 0.69, p<0.001; PFS: HR=1.83, 95% CI 1.43 to 2.33, p<0.001; OS: HR=1.35, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.77, p=0.03) or KRASmut/KEAP1mut (ORR: OR=0.37, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.64, p<0.001; PFS: HR=2.09, 95% CI 1.61 to 2.71, p<0.001; OS: HR=1.84, 95% CI 1.39 to 2.44, p<0.001, online supplemental tables 33–35) had the worst clinical outcomes, independent of smoking history. These findings demonstrate that although these mutations are more frequently observed in patients with smoking history, they independently predict IO-based treatment outcomes in advanced NSCLC.
Differential benefits of first-line chemo-IO versus IO alone with regards to smoking history among patients with PD-L1 TPS of ≥50% lacking EGFR/ALK alterations
In patients with PD-L1 TPS of ≥50% NSCLC lacking EGFR/ALK alterations, both chemo-IO and IO alone are approved first-line treatments. Our analysis revealed distinct treatment benefits based on smoking history. Among patients who had never smoked (n=66), first-line chemo-IO demonstrated improved clinical outcomes compared with IO alone, with higher response rates (70.0% vs 23.9%, p=0.001, figure 4A), prolonged PFS (mPFS 9.5 vs 3.7 months, HR=0.51, 95% CI 0.27 to 0.95, p=0.04, figure 4B), and a trend toward prolonged OS (mOS 22.3 vs 18.5 months, HR=0.71, 95% CI 0.35 to 1.47, p=0.36, figure 4C). In contrast, among patients with a smoking history (n=574), the modest improvement in response with chemo-IO (53.7% vs 42.3%, p=0.04, figure 4D) did not translate into significant long-term survival benefits (mPFS: 10.7 vs 5.88 months, HR=0.79, 95% CI 0.61 to 1.01, p=0.06; mOS: 26.2 vs 21.4 months, HR=0.92, 95% CI 0.68 to 1.23, p=0.56, figure 4E,F). Multivariable analysis confirmed the selective PFS benefit of chemo-IO in patients who had never smoked (HR=0.51, 95% CI 0.29 to 0.92, p=0.03, online supplemental tables 36–41), with this benefit becoming more pronounced at higher PD-L1 TPS levels of 50–89% (HR=0.30, 95% CI 0.15 to 0.59, p<0.001, online supplemental tables 42–47) and of ≥90% (online supplemental figure 2).
Tobacco smoking-related mutational signature as an independent predictive biomarker for immunotherapy
Beyond self-reported smoking history, we investigated tobacco smoking-related mutational signature (TSMS) as a potential biomarker for IO. Although TSMS enrichment correlated with self-reported smoking status, it was notably absent in 56.2% of the former and 40.3% of the patients who smokes. TSMS enrichment showed a dose-dependent relationship with cumulative smoking PYs (χ2 trend test p<0.001) and provided molecular smoking information for 16% of patients with an unknown smoking history (figure 5A,B). Moreover, TSMS enrichment independently predicted better outcomes in patients receiving IO alone, with higher ORR (OR=2.32, 95% CI 1.52 to 3.57, p<0.001, figure 5C, online supplemental table 48) and longer PFS (HR=0.64, 95% CI 0.51 to 0.81, p<0.001, figure 5D, online supplemental table 49) and OS (HR=0.71, 95% CI 0.55 to 0.93, p=0.01, figure 5E, online supplemental table 50), and the associations remained significant after TMB adjustment (online supplemental tables 51–53). Moreover, TSMS enrichment even provided predictive value in patients who have quit smoking for more than 12 months (online supplemental tables 54–56), suggesting its potential ability to detect durable smoking-related molecular alterations relevant to ICI response.
Smoking history is associated with established clinical biomarkers
To understand the mechanisms underlying the varied IO treatment responses and outcomes, we first analyzed established clinical biomarkers. Patients who were actively smoking exhibited the highest PD-L1 TPS (median PD-L1 TPS=20%, PD-L1 TPS of ≥50%: 39.1%, online supplemental figure 3A, online supplemental tables 57,58) compared with patients who do not smoke, but showed no association with smoking intensity (figure 6A). In contrast, TMB demonstrated a positive correlation with smoking PYs: patients with heavy tobacco use (≥40 PYs) showed the highest TMB (median TMB (mTMB)=11.41 mut/Mb), followed by moderate (mTMB=10.65 mut/Mb) and light use (mTMB=9.13 mut/Mb), while patients who do not smoke had the lowest (mTMB=6.84 mut/Mb) (p<0.001, figure 6B, online supplemental figure 3B). Smoking status or intensity was not significantly associated with dNLR (figure 6C, online supplemental figure 3C).
Smoking history is associated with emerging biomarkers
Analysis of immune cell infiltration in 619 NSCLC samples at the DFCI demonstrated significant dose-response relationships between smoking intensity and increased median intratumoral immune cell counts. CD8+ cell counts increased progressively with smoking intensity (never: 140.8, light: 175.8, moderate: 207.0, heavy: 220.0 count/mm², p<0.001), as did PD-1+ (never: 56.3, light: 74.9, moderate: 80.3, heavy: 106.0 count/mm², p<0.001), CD8+PD-1+ (never: 10.1, light: 13.3, moderate: 17.5, heavy: 25.9 count/mm², p<0.001), and FOXP3+ cells (never: 51.7, light: 63.7, moderate: 71.7, heavy: 70.0 count/mm², p<0.001). Similar associations were observed at the tumor-stroma interface and in the combined total region (figure 7A, online supplemental figure 4), (online supplemental tables 59,60).
In adjusted DEP analysis of 152 DFCI samples, we identified nine plasma proteins significantly elevated in tobacco users: P4HB (OR=1.38), CDCP1 (OR=1.86), CCN4 (OR=1.61), CCL7 (OR=2.55), CCDC134 (OR=2.76), TNFRSF6B (OR=2.19), CXCL17 (OR=2.03), MLN (OR=3.74), and MRC1 (OR=1.59) (figure 7B, online supplemental table 61). These proteins showed a gradient pattern based on smoking history (figure 7C). Notably, CDCP1 independently predicted improved response to IO monotherapy (HR=2.73, 95% CI 1.39 to 5.87, p=0.006, (online supplemental figure 6). Pathway enrichment analysis revealed overrepresentation of chemokine receptor, peptide ligand binding, and G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) ligand binding pathways (online supplemental figure 7).
Lastly, analysis of bulk RNA sequencing data from 111 lung adenocarcinoma samples revealed that tobacco use was associated with increased CD4 memory activated T cells and upregulated pathways including oxidative phosphorylation, glutathione metabolism, exosomal secretion and extracellular vesicle biogenesis (online supplemental table 62, onlinesupplemental figures 8 9). Collectively, these findings suggest that tobacco smoking in NSCLC is associated with increased immune cell infiltration, tobacco smoking-related circulating proteomic profiles, and gene expression signatures in cancer metabolism and signaling transport, which may enhance sensitivity to ICI.
Discussion
In this multicenter study of patients with advanced NSCLC receiving IO with or without chemotherapy, we demonstrate that detailed smoking history provides crucial insights for treatment selection beyond the classification of never, former and current smoking status. This observation is supported by comprehensive multi-omics analyses integrated with clinical outcomes in large numbers of patients. Our findings reveal differential benefits between IO alone and chemo-IO based on specific smoking history, particularly in patients with high PD-L1 expression. Furthermore, we show that both smoking status and intensity significantly influence the tumor immune microenvironment and induce systemic changes in plasma proteomic profiles.
Consistent with our previous work,1 2 patients with a smoking history, particularly those with heavy tobacco use, showed improved response and survival outcomes with IO alone compared with patients who do not smoke in this expanded patient population. However, the impact of smoking history on chemo-IO outcomes follows a distinct pattern. While smoking status and intensity did not affect the initial response to chemo-IO, patients who were actively smoking demonstrated prolonged PFS, with those reporting heavy tobacco use (≥40 PYs) experiencing the most significant long-term benefits in both measures.11 The comparable initial response rates regardless of smoking status may be attributed to the chemotherapy component. There is evidence that non-smoking-enriched molecular subtypes of NSCLC, such as those with EGFR or ALK alterations, may exhibit increased sensitivity to pemetrexed through mechanisms involving reduced thymidylate synthase expression.33 34 Meanwhile, the long-term survival advantage observed in patients with a smoking history likely depends on the IO maintenance component, consistent with the pattern seen with IO monotherapy. This suggests that while chemotherapy may enhance the initial IO response in patients who do not smoke, the sustained benefit of IO maintenance remains predominantly effective in those with a smoking history, presumably due to their higher TMB and tumor-infiltrating immune cells.
In the first-line setting for patients with PD-L1 TPS of ≥50% lacking EGFR/ALK alterations, the benefit of treatment intensification varies according to smoking history. Patients who do not smoke derived a significant survival benefit from chemo-IO compared with IO alone, while patients with a smoking history showed comparable outcomes with either strategy. These findings have significant clinical implications for treatment selection, as both IO monotherapy and chemo-IO are approved first-line options for this important patient subgroup. While our data suggest smoking history may influence treatment outcomes in patients with high PD-L1 expression, randomized controlled trials are needed to determine whether smoking status should guide treatment selection. Notably, this pattern was observed across PD-L1 expression levels, including subgroups with PD-L1 TPS of 50–89% and ≥90%, suggesting consistency in the association, which aligns with prior work.11 These results highlight smoking history as a potentially important clinical variable that warrants further investigation alongside molecular tumor characteristics in treatment decision-making, though prospective validation in larger, independent cohorts is essential before any clinical recommendations can be established.
The improved clinical outcomes in patients with tobacco use can be explained by mechanistic associations. Patients who were actively smoking showed the highest PD-L1 TPS, though the underlying mechanisms remain unclear with conflicting evidence regarding the impact of smoking status and intensity.135,39 These inconsistent PD-L1 TPS findings warrant careful interpretation owing to several limitations: technical variability in clinical PD-L1 IHC quantification, lack of standardization across assays and pathologists, heterogeneous definitions of smoking history, and differences in tumor sample quality and molecular characteristics across studies.40 In contrast, TMB demonstrates a consistent dose-response relationship with both smoking status and intensity.1 13 The favorable IO outcomes likely reflect tobacco-induced increases in tumor mutations and neoantigens combined with T-cell proinflammatory cytokines that are known to induce PD-L1 expression.41
Additionally, we observed increased immune cell infiltration that correlated with smoking intensity, particularly CD8+ and PD-1+ cells, suggesting enhanced immune recognition in smoking-associated tumors.13 42 However, we acknowledge that the observed CD8+PD-1+ populations likely represent a heterogeneous composition of activated and exhausted T cell subsets. Future studies incorporating additional markers would be important to characterize the functional state of these infiltrating T cells. Analysis of circulating proteins identified several key molecules, including tumor necrosis factor-receptor TNFRSF6B; chemokines CCL7 and CXCL17; and cell signaling and immune response proteins CDCP1, NOS3, and MRC1. Notably, elevated levels of circulating TNFRSF6B and CDCP1 have been validated as strong risk factors for lung cancer incidence, with CDCP1’s association with smoking exposure reported previously.28 43 44 Our study extends these findings by demonstrating that tobacco exposure has potentially reversible systemic effects on circulating proteins in patients with advanced lung cancer. The enrichment of proteins involved in chemokine signaling and peptide binding pathways not only provides potential mechanisms linking smoking history to treatment response but also holds promise as a non-invasive predictive biomarker for IO. However, these associations are observational and independent validation in separate cohorts as well as mechanistic studies is warranted.
The TSMS derived from OncoPanel independently predicted IO alone outcomes in lung adenocarcinoma, even after adjusting for TMB. While TSMS and TMB are correlated, TSMS may capture more specific biological mechanisms related to tobacco-induced mutations, such as transversion events, whereas TMB encompasses broader mutational processes, including age-related changes and chronic inflammation, mechanisms that can coexist and occur independently of documented smoking history.13 39 45 However, our TSMS analysis was limited to patients with lung adenocarcinoma due to insufficient cases with comprehensive genomic data, and validation in other histologic subtypes is needed. Given the widespread clinical use of panel-based NGS, TSMS hold the promise to reduce smoking stigma and serve as a biomarker for IO, complementing self-reported smoking history.46 47
This study had several limitations. Although our study included a large cohort, patients who do not smoke with high PD-L1 expression lacking EGFR/ALK alterations represent a naturally small patient population, limiting the statistical power of certain subgroup analyses. Sample sizes for emerging molecular biomarkers, such as plasma proteins and tumor transcriptomics, were restricted, and mutational signature analysis could only be performed in DFCI patients for whom detailed genomic data were available. Additionally, we did not systematically capture smoking-related comorbidities such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, which may influence IO response through altered systemic inflammation and immune function.48 Moreover, smoking is known to alter airway and gut microbiomes, which have been increasingly implicated in modulating IO response,49 representing another potential mechanistic pathway that we could not evaluate in our study. Furthermore, as this was a real-world analysis, follow-up patterns varied among patients, which could potentially affect PFS estimates compared with standardized clinical trial assessments. Given the retrospective design, prospective validation in other independent cohorts is needed for generalizable conclusions.
In conclusion, our study provides a comprehensive analysis of how cigarette smoking history influences IO outcomes in NSCLC via complex molecular mechanisms. These findings have clinical implications for personalized treatment selection and suggest new directions for biomarker development.
